answer:
Make the latency budget explicit from keystroke to visible completion: debounce/network, context selection, prefill, and first useful output. Under a sub-150ms p95 target, use a nearby small code model, short bounded context, cached repository summaries, and aggressive cancellation of stale requests. A distant large model with cold prefill may simply not meet the target; measure components before promising it.

Context includes prefix/suffix around the cursor, imports, nearby definitions, selected open files, and retrieved symbols with repository permissions. Build a fill-in-the-middle prompt using the model’s actual training format. Cache AST/symbol indexes incrementally by file version; never reuse a completion after its surrounding code changes without revalidation.

Speculative decoding can reduce expensive verification rounds when draft acceptance is high, but draft overhead can lose at short completions. Stream complete useful fragments, suppress obviously invalid insertions, and stop on edit/cursor changes. Evaluate acceptance and accepted characters, edit distance after acceptance, syntax/test outcomes, latency, and distraction rate. Randomize experiments by user/repository to limit contamination from repeated suggestions.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** End-to-end latency includes context preparation, network transit, prefill, decoding, and rendering. These components may overlap, so use traces instead of summing unrelated percentile measurements. Cache reusable prefixes and cancel stale work; otherwise a high-throughput backend can spend most of its capacity generating suggestions the user has already made irrelevant. For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/how-github-copilot-is-getting-better-at-understanding-your-code/) and [2](https://github.blog/2023-05-17-inside-github-working-with-the-llms-behind-github-copilot/).
